1.title: Scope, Schedule and Cost
1.text: Welcome to Module 7. Scope, schedule and cost are the classic triple constraint, and they are tightly linked: a change in one moves the others. This module covers all three. In Part 1, we start with scope: how to define it, structure it, control it and get it accepted. Part 2 covers the schedule, including the critical path. Part 3 covers cost: budgets, reserves and earned value.

1.title: Where This Module Sits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits. The Process domain has ten tasks, and this module covers three. Task two: develop and manage scope. Task eight: plan and manage schedule. Task six: plan and manage finance. Each has a part. Remember that the three are tightly linked. A scope change hits schedule and cost immediately. So the best answer often asks how a change in one affects the other two, and routes it through the right control.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Elicit requirements, write the scope statement and build the work breakdown structure or backlog. Control scope: creep, gold plating, verification and validation. Build the schedule: logic, estimates, the critical path, float and compression. Forecast and control the schedule in predictive, agile and hybrid work. Build the budget, reserves and cost baseline. And use earned value to forecast and respond to variances.

1.title: Case Check-In: The Microgrid's Scope
1.text: Our microgrid has a clear scope. The deliverables are six megawatts of solar canopies, four megawatt hours of battery storage, the controller and switchgear, and the dashboard. Project management work is in scope too. Campus-wide building retrofits and electric vehicle charging stations are out of scope. Writing exclusions down manages expectations and reduces scope creep. Acceptance criteria will say when each deliverable counts as accepted. The scope statement, work breakdown structure and dictionary together form the scope baseline.

1.title: Scope: Key Terms
1.text: Key terms. Product scope covers the features and functions of the product. Project scope is the work needed to deliver it. A requirement is a condition or capability that must be present to satisfy a business need. A deliverable is a unique, verifiable product, result or capability. The scope baseline is the approved scope statement, work breakdown structure and WBS dictionary. Scope creep is uncontrolled expansion without adjustments to time, cost and resources. Verification checks the deliverable is built correctly. Validation checks that the customer accepts it.

1.title: The Six Scope Processes
1.text: There are six scope processes. Four are in Planning. Plan Scope Management produces the scope and requirements management plans. Elicit and Analyze Requirements produces requirements documentation. Define Scope produces the project scope statement. Develop Scope Structure produces the scope baseline, and in adaptive work the backlog. Two are in Monitoring and Controlling. Monitor and Control Scope produces verified deliverables and manages changes. Validate Scope produces accepted deliverables. Note the difference: verified, then accepted.

1.title: Plan Scope Management
1.text: Plan Scope Management produces two plans. The scope management plan describes how the project scope statement is prepared and how the work breakdown structure is created. It also describes how the scope baseline is approved and maintained, and how formal acceptance is obtained. The requirements management plan, sometimes called a business analysis plan, describes how requirements are analyzed, documented and managed, including prioritization, change authorization and traceability. Both can be formal or informal. Adaptive scope management is more iterative and collaborative.

1.title: Eliciting Requirements
1.text: Elicitation techniques fit different situations. Interviews are direct and individual, ideal for experts, executives and confidential topics. Focus groups bring prequalified stakeholders together under a moderator. Surveys reach many respondents quickly. Observation, or job shadowing, uncovers hidden requirements when users cannot or will not articulate their needs. The nominal group technique has everyone contribute before discussion, which limits dominant voices. Prototypes and design thinking give early feedback. Document analysis and benchmarking draw on contracts, regulations and comparable organizations.

1.title: Practical Rules for Requirements
1.text: Some practical rules. Before baselining, a requirement should be unambiguous, measurable and testable, traceable, complete, consistent and acceptable to key stakeholders. If requirements conflict, make the conflict visible to everyone involved and discuss the trade-offs together. Do not just rank them or pick the senior person's request. If a goal is vague, such as improve engagement, agree measurable outcomes first. If signed requirements are read differently, facilitate a discussion. And treat compliance and sustainability needs as requirements.

1.title: Requirements Traceability
1.text: A requirements traceability matrix links each requirement from its origin to the deliverable that satisfies it, and onward to design, test and acceptance. It shows that every approved requirement is delivered, that each adds business value, and it structures change management of product scope. Typical attributes: identifier, source, priority, owner, status and acceptance criteria. If a requirement links to no business objective, confirm with stakeholders whether it belongs in scope. Do not attach it to the nearest objective to finish the matrix. That fakes traceability.

1.title: Define Scope: The Scope Statement
1.text: The project scope statement is a detailed description of the project and product scope. It gives a common understanding among stakeholders, and it is the baseline for judging whether a request is inside or outside the project's boundaries. It contains the scope description, the deliverables, the acceptance criteria, the exclusions, and the assumptions and constraints. Define Scope also identifies quality requirements and standards. The charter has high-level information. The scope statement is the detailed description. In adaptive work, scope is described at a high level, as a roadmap with releases.

1.title: Obtaining Stakeholder Agreement on Scope
1.text: Obtaining stakeholder agreement has four steps. Review the scope statement, requirements, exclusions and acceptance criteria with key stakeholders and the sponsor. Surface and resolve conflicting or unstated expectations before the scope is approved. Obtain documented approval. The approved documents form the baseline. In adaptive work, agree the vision, the minimum viable product, the prioritization criteria and the definition of done at planning events. The product owner is the voice for scope decisions, and stakeholder feedback is built into every iteration.

1.title: The Work Breakdown Structure
1.text: The work breakdown structure is a hierarchical decomposition of the total scope into deliverables and work packages. Our microgrid has five top-level branches: solar canopies, battery storage, the controller, the dashboard and project management. The hundred percent rule says the WBS contains all product and project work, including project management, and nothing more. Branches name what is produced, deliverables, and activities come later in the schedule. Work packages are the lowest level, and they are estimable, assignable and controllable.

1.title: WBS Rules and Structure
1.text: A few WBS rules. Decompose to the right depth: components must be necessary and sufficient for the parent deliverable, and estimable, assignable and controllable. Too much decomposition wastes effort and causes roll-up problems. Far-future work that cannot be decomposed yet stays as a planning package, and is detailed later. The WBS dictionary describes each element: description of work, assumptions, responsible party, milestones, cost, quality requirements and acceptance criteria. A control account is a management control point that integrates scope, budget and schedule.

1.title: Adaptive Scope Structure
1.text: In adaptive work, the product backlog corresponds to the work breakdown structure. Work items break down into epics, features and user stories, ordered by value. An epic is a large body of related work. A feature is a set of related requirements that provides value. A user story states an outcome from a stakeholder's perspective. The scope baseline is defined at the start of each iteration, and usually the product owner approves changes dynamically, without formal change control. A value breakdown structure lets a team rank deliverables by expected value.

1.title: Is It a Scope Change?
1.text: Not every discovery is a change. If work is already in the signed scope but missing from the work breakdown structure, add it. It is not a change, so no change request is needed. If a stakeholder asks for a new feature outside the baseline, it is a change. Predictive work uses a change request and impact assessment. Adaptive work uses the product owner and the backlog. If the team wants to add an unrequested extra to delight the customer, that is gold plating: do not deliver it unapproved. More detail inside agreed scope is progressive elaboration, not change.

1.title: Monitor and Control Scope
1.text: Monitor and Control Scope compares actual results with the baseline or backlog, manages changes, and measures the quality and value of deliverables. Tools include variance, trend and root cause analysis, audits and inspections. In adaptive work, backlog management and refinement keep scope current. A burnup chart shows scope added against work completed, so growing scope is not mistaken for a slow team. If a vendor delivers more than specified, even for free, evaluate the impact and process it through change control. Control formally even when the change is good.

1.title: Verify, Then Validate
1.text: Verification and validation are different. Verification asks: is it built correctly, does it comply with the requirement, specification and quality standard? The project team and quality function do it, and the output is verified deliverables. If it fails, repair the defect and re-inspect. Validation asks: is it what the customer needs, and do they accept it? The customer, sponsor or authorized acceptor does it, and the output is accepted deliverables. If it fails, a change request or rework follows, and acceptance is withheld. Verified is not accepted.

1.title: Validate Scope
1.text: Validate Scope checks the processes used to reach quality standards and formalizes acceptance. Tools include inspection, customer talks and tests, and review meetings. Transition readiness matters: scope can be complete while the receiving team is not ready, for example when support staff are not trained, so validate readiness before handover. Accepted deliverables feed closure, and each phase closes formally. In adaptive work, a sprint review validates each increment against the definition of done and the story's acceptance criteria. Do not close a phase on technical completion alone.

1.title: Scope, Quality and Sustainability
1.text: Quality is a feature of scope. Functional and nonfunctional requirements and target thresholds trade off with cost and schedule like any other scope. Define Scope captures quality requirements, Monitor and Control Scope measures them, and Validate Scope checks quality processes and obtains acceptance. A customer-required sustainability criterion, such as water-use certification, is a quality requirement, and the work breakdown structure or backlog should include work to manage sustainability. For metrics, scope creep is unplanned deliverables over total, and requirements stability is unchanged requirements over total.

1.title: Scope in Predictive, Agile and Hybrid Work
1.text: Scope differs by approach. Predictive: detailed up front, with a work breakdown structure and dictionary. A baseline changed only through formal change control. Priorities of mandatory against optional. And formal acceptance. Agile: high-level scope and a product backlog. A baseline per iteration, with the product owner approving changes. Value-based ordering. And acceptance through the definition of done and sprint reviews. Hybrid: a baseline for the committed envelope and a backlog for the evolving parts. With a fixed date and uncertain scope, fix the date and deliver prioritized increments.

1.title: Scope Traps: What PMI Expects
1.text: The traps for scope. Already in agreed scope but missing from the work breakdown structure? Add it, with no change request. A change request is for work outside the baseline. Verified is not accepted, so define acceptance criteria and exclusions up front. Make conflicting requirements visible and resolve them together. No gold plating: even a free upgrade goes through impact assessment and change control. Decompose to the right level, and remember the work breakdown structure covers one hundred percent of scope. In agile work, route new requests to the backlog.

1.title: Part 1 Recap
1.text: Let us recap Part 1. Requirements are elicited, traceable and tied to acceptance criteria. The scope statement holds deliverables, acceptance criteria and exclusions, agreed with stakeholders before baselining. The work breakdown structure or backlog follows the hundred percent rule, the right depth and rolling wave planning. For control, in-scope omissions are added, and new requests go through change control or the product owner. Verify, then validate, with formal acceptance and transition readiness. And quality and sustainability are part of scope. In Part 2, we turn to the schedule.

2.title: Schedule: Key Terms
2.text: Part 2 covers the schedule. Key terms. The schedule model represents the plan for executing activities. The schedule baseline is the approved version, changed only through change control. A milestone is a significant point with zero duration. Effort is the labor units needed, and duration is the work periods needed to complete an activity. The critical path is the longest path, and it determines the shortest possible project duration. Float is the room to delay. A lead lets a successor start earlier, a lag delays it. And a schedule reserve is visible time protecting the date from uncertainty.

2.title: The Three Schedule Processes
2.text: Three schedule processes. Plan Schedule Management sets policies, procedures and documentation, and produces the schedule management plan. Develop Schedule analyzes sequences, durations, resources and constraints to create the schedule model, and produces the schedule baseline and the project schedule. Monitor and Control Schedule tracks status, updates the schedule, and manages changes to the baseline, producing schedule forecasts and change requests. Any change to the baseline or agreed schedule goes through integrated change control.

2.title: Plan Schedule Management
2.text: The schedule management plan defines how the schedule is developed, monitored and controlled. It sets the scheduling method and tool, and the release and iteration length. It sets the level of accuracy and units of measure. It sets control thresholds that trigger action. It also sets rules of performance measurement, such as percent complete and earned value, and reporting formats. Timeboxing minimizes scope creep by forcing essential features first. Prepare the schedule to match the approach: milestones, dependencies and critical paths for predictive, timeboxed schedules for adaptive, and milestones with iterations beneath for hybrid.

2.title: Develop Schedule: Four Steps
2.text: Developing the schedule has four steps. Define activities: decompose work packages into activities that can be estimated, scheduled and controlled. Determine sequence: logical relationships between activities. Estimate effort and duration, using the people most familiar with the work. Adjust. If the draft is unacceptable, apply compression, resource optimization, reserves or alternative logic. And confirm dates do not clash with calendars or other projects. Then resolve conflicts, involve stakeholders, approve and baseline. Where detail is unknown, use rolling wave planning.

2.title: Logical Relationships
2.text: Four logical relationships. Finish-to-start: the successor starts after the predecessor finishes. This is the most common. Start-to-start: the successor starts after the predecessor starts. Finish-to-finish: the successor finishes after the predecessor finishes. Start-to-finish: the successor finishes after the predecessor starts. It is rare. A lag delays the successor, a lead lets it start earlier, and neither should replace the schedule logic. Every activity except the first and last needs a predecessor and a successor, and closed loops must be avoided.

2.title: Estimating Durations
2.text: Estimating durations. People most familiar with the work estimate, using resource calendars. Some work has a fixed duration regardless of resources, like a twenty-four-hour stress test. Doubling resources does not halve duration, because of diminishing returns, learning curves and coordination. Record the assumptions and data behind each estimate. Watch for cognitive bias such as the planning fallacy. Historical data and benchmarks support analogous and parametric estimates, and they are reliable when the data are accurate, the parameters quantifiable and the model scalable.

2.title: Critical Path Method
2.text: Here is a worked example. Activity A takes three days. It is followed by B, four days, and C, six days, which run in parallel. Both feed D, two days, then E, three days. Forward pass: A runs days one to three. B runs four to seven. C runs four to nine. D starts day ten and finishes day eleven. E runs twelve to fourteen. The longest path is A, C, D, E: fourteen days. That is the critical path. Backward pass shows B can slip two days: total float two. PMBOK 8 uses the day-one convention.

2.title: Float
2.text: Float is the room to delay. Total float is the delay possible without delaying the project finish date or violating a constraint. It equals late start minus early start. Free float is the delay possible without delaying the early start of a successor. Negative float occurs when constraints demand dates earlier than the logic and durations allow. In our example, activity B has total float of two, and free float of two. The critical path has normally zero total float. Total float is shared along a path.

2.title: Schedule Compression
2.text: Compression shortens the schedule without reducing scope. Crashing adds resources, such as overtime, extra people or expedited delivery. It raises cost, and may not produce a viable result. Fast tracking does in parallel what was planned in sequence. It adds rework and quality risk, coordination effort and possibly cost. Only compressing critical-path activities shortens the finish date. Do not add resources to a non-critical activity to recover a late project. Pick by cost and risk, and use change control if the baseline changes.

2.title: Resource Leveling and Smoothing
2.text: Resource optimization has two techniques. Resource leveling moves dates to balance demand with supply, when resources are over-allocated or limited. It may change the critical path and delay the end date. Resource smoothing uses free and total float only, so the critical path and end date are unchanged, though it may not solve every peak. So for an over-allocation on non-critical activities, smooth within float first. It costs nothing. Leveling can move the end date.

2.title: Other Schedule Analysis Tools
2.text: Other tools help. The critical chain method, based on the theory of constraints, replaces task-level buffers with one project buffer and feeding buffers on a resource-leveled critical path. What-if scenario analysis computes schedules under scenarios such as a late delivery, a strike or a permit change, and helps size reserves. Simulation gives the probability of meeting a date. Reserve analysis asks whether reserves are sufficient for the remaining risk. Critical path drag, from PMBOK 8, is how much time a critical activity adds to the project.

2.title: The Schedule Baseline
2.text: After conflicts are resolved and stakeholders approve, the schedule model becomes the schedule baseline, with baseline start and finish dates. The working project schedule is then updated with actuals and forecasts, while the baseline stays fixed. Together with the scope and cost baselines, it forms the performance measurement baseline. Changes to the baseline, even corrections of errors, go through change control. Check dates against resource calendars and other projects. A schedule forecast is a prediction of future conditions based on current progress, and it is reissued as work performance data arrive.

2.title: Coordinate With Other Projects and Operations
2.text: Coordinate with other projects and operations. External dependencies, such as permits, utility connections and other projects' deliverables. Identify them. Agree dates with the owners. Show them as milestones or constraints. And track them as risks. Shared resources: check calendars and competing assignments, and agree release dates with functional managers or the PMO. Operations constraints, such as change freezes and outage windows, belong in the schedule as constraints. Align release dates through the program, and escalate conflicts beyond your authority.

2.title: Case Check-In: The Microgrid Schedule
2.text: Our microgrid schedule has a clear external dependency. Permit approval and the utility interconnection are not controlled by the team. Agree dates with the Planning and Permits Office and the utility, show them as milestones, and track them as risks. Battery lead time drives procurement. Construction is on the critical path. Commissioning is a zero-duration milestone. Beneath, the software lane runs in two-week iterations. Executives see milestones, and the team plans iterations beneath them.

2.title: Agile Scheduling
2.text: Adaptive scheduling works in layers. A roadmap gives vision and themes. A release plan, typically three to six months, is a high-level timeline that fixes the number of iterations and shows which features arrive when. An iteration plan is a detailed plan for the current iteration, two weeks to a month, with stories in points and tasks in hours. Fix time and cost, and flex scope: deliver prioritized increments. The iteration length does not stretch to absorb unfinished work.

2.title: Forecasting With Velocity
2.text: Velocity is the rate at which deliverables are produced, validated and accepted per iteration. As exam practice, forecast with remaining backlog divided by velocity. With one hundred twenty points remaining and a velocity of twenty-four, that is five iterations, ten weeks at two weeks each. Use a range of velocities for a range of dates, and refine as data accumulate. A burnup chart shows scope growth. If scope rises as fast as work completes, the team is delivering steadily while scope grows. Velocity is output, not value.

2.title: Hybrid and Other Scheduling Approaches
2.text: In hybrid work, executives see milestones with iteration plans beneath them. A detailed Gantt chart built from a backlog adds false precision, so avoid it. Some streams may use Kanban or the critical path method. PMBOK 8 also describes location-based scheduling, with quantities allocated to locations, production rates and crew sizes. It describes lean scheduling too, with pull planning, look-ahead planning and the Last Planner System. Keep each element's schedule at a commensurate level of detail. And do not send every iteration change through a change board.

2.title: Monitor and Control the Schedule
2.text: When the schedule varies, respond in five steps. Find the cause, using root cause analysis. Check the effect on the critical path and float. An SPI below one on work with large float may not threaten the finish date, while delay on the critical path does. Evaluate options: crash, fast track, re-sequence, use or reassess reserves, reduce scope through change control, or escalate if beyond your authority. Use change control when the baseline would change. Update forecasts and communicate. In adaptive work, compare work delivered and accepted with estimates.

2.title: Schedule Variance Measures
2.text: Schedule variance is earned value minus planned value. Negative means behind plan. The schedule performance index is earned value divided by planned value. Below one means behind, above one ahead. Variance analysis compares baseline with actual, reviewing cause and degree. Trend analysis projects future results from history, an early warning of slippage. But do not stop at the index: analyze the critical path and float before deciding that the end date is at risk. Contracted work needs regular status updates and reviews to confirm supplier reports.

2.title: Schedule in Predictive, Agile and Hybrid Work
2.text: Schedule looks different by approach. Predictive: a detailed schedule with a network and critical path, and parametric or bottom-up estimates. Control is baseline against actual, with schedule variance and the index. Tools include the critical path method, crashing and fast tracking. Agile: roadmap, release and iteration plans. Story points and velocity. Control through delivered and accepted work and burn charts. And a fixed timebox with flexible scope. Hybrid: milestones on top, iterations beneath. Use relative sizing for uncertain agile work.

2.title: Schedule Traps: What PMI Expects
2.text: The traps for schedule. Only critical-path compression shortens the finish date. Crashing costs money, fast tracking adds risk, and neither cuts scope. Smooth within float first, because leveling can move the end date. More people do not shorten work in proportion. Padding is not a reserve, and external dependencies and operations constraints belong in the schedule. Baseline changes, even corrections of errors, go through change control. In agile work, fix the timebox and flex scope. When two stakeholders expect different dates, facilitate agreement.

2.title: Finance: Key Terms
2.text: Part 2 ends with the vocabulary for finance, which Part 3 develops. Funding is how the project gets its money. Capital expenditure is investment in assets, and operating expenditure is day-to-day running cost. A cost estimate is the likely cost of resources for an activity. The cost baseline is the approved time-phased budget, excluding management reserve. The performance measurement baseline is the scope, schedule and cost baselines together. Budget at completion is the total planned value. Life cycle cost includes later cost of use, maintenance and support.

2.title: The Four Finance Processes
2.text: Four finance processes. Plan Financial Management defines how revenues and expenses will be estimated, budgeted, managed and controlled, and produces the financial management plan and funding strategy. Estimate Costs approximates the cost of resources needed. Develop Budget aggregates estimates into an authorized cost baseline. Monitor and Control Finances tracks spending, manages changes to the baseline and forecasts, and keeps the project financially viable. The domain aims at value, not only low cost.

2.title: Plan Financial Management
2.text: The financial management plan describes how costs will be planned, structured and controlled. It sets units of measure and the level of precision. It sets the level of accuracy, such as plus or minus ten percent. And it sets control accounts, which link WBS components to the accounting system. It sets control thresholds, rules of performance measurement including how the estimate at completion is calculated, reporting formats, and procedures for currency fluctuations. Define who gets which reports. If the board requires earned value data, adapt the reporting.

2.title: Part 2 Recap
2.text: Let us recap Part 2. The schedule baseline comes from logic, estimates and adjustments, and changes only through change control. On the critical path, only critical compression shortens the finish. Crash, fast track, level or smooth, by cost and risk. Agile and hybrid scheduling use timeboxes, velocity forecasts, and milestones with iterations beneath. When a variance appears, find the cause, check the critical path, evaluate options, and use change control. And we met the finance basics: baseline, budget at completion, capital and operating expenditure, and the financial management plan. In Part 3, we turn to funding, budgets and earned value.

3.title: Funding and Financial Needs
3.text: Analyze financial needs. How much money and when? Funding requirements come from the cost baseline, often incremental and uneven. From where? Choose a funding strategy: internal budgets, a client contract, incremental disbursement, external investment, grants or crowdfunding. Under what constraints? Capital or operating expenditure, fiscal-year limits and grant conditions. What value is expected? And what will it cost over the product's life? Plan spend tracking by deciding when cost is recognized: committed, ordered, delivered or incurred.

3.title: Estimate Costs
3.text: Estimate costs for all resources charged to the project: labor, materials, equipment, services and facilities. Add special categories, such as an inflation allowance, the cost of financing and contingency. Techniques include expert judgment, analogous, parametric, bottom-up and three-point estimating, plus the constructive cost model for software. Consider alternatives: make or buy, buy or lease, share resources. Outputs are the cost estimates and the basis of estimates. Estimates are refined as the project progresses, and accuracy improves.

3.title: Cost of Quality
3.text: Cost of quality has two sides. The cost of conformance is money spent to avoid failures. That includes prevention, such as training, documented processes and doing it right. And it includes appraisal, such as testing and inspection. The cost of nonconformance is money spent because of failures. Internal failure is found by the project, such as rework and scrap. External failure is found by the customer, such as warranty, liability and lost business. Prevention costs less than appraisal and failure. There is an optimal level where extra prevention stops paying off.

3.title: Develop the Budget
3.text: Develop Budget aggregates work package estimates to control accounts and then the project total. Reserve analysis and historical information review refine the budget. If planned spending exceeds a funding limit, funding limit reconciliation reschedules work to level out the rate of spending, or obtains more funds. Work cost estimates plus contingency form the cost baseline, the approved time-phased budget. Management reserve is added on top for funding. Reserves may be managed implicitly, inside the budget, or explicitly, tracked apart.

3.title: The Cost Baseline as an S-Curve
3.text: The cost baseline is a time-phased budget, usually drawn as an S-curve. Cumulative planned spend starts slowly, rises fastest in the middle of the project, and tapers as it approaches the budget at completion. Project funding requirements follow from the baseline, including contingency, and total funds equal the cost baseline plus the management reserve. Together with the scope and schedule baselines, the cost baseline forms the performance measurement baseline, used to measure and control execution. It changes only through formal change control.

3.title: Contingency Versus Management Reserve
3.text: Two reserves, two purposes. A contingency reserve covers known risks with active response strategies, the known unknowns. It sits in the cost or schedule baseline, and is released per the reserve protocols in the risk management plan. It can be sized by a percentage, a fixed amount or quantitative analysis. A management reserve covers unforeseen work within scope, the unknown unknowns. It is in addition to the baseline, never part of it, and is usually released by senior management. Show contingency clearly. Do not hide it in estimates.

3.title: Managing Reserves
3.text: How to manage reserves. Use contingency when identified risks occur, and reduce or release it as risks pass. Use management reserve only for unforeseen in-scope work, through the approval path the organization sets. Using it normally needs a change request, so the baseline reflects the new authorization. If reserves burn faster than progress, that is a governance signal: reassess adequacy against remaining risks and tell the sponsor. Do not quietly top up from management reserve. Small and government projects often hold larger buffers. As an example, expected values of thirty, twenty and twenty thousand suggest about seventy thousand of contingency.

3.title: Case Check-In: Reserves on the Microgrid
3.text: Back to our microgrid budget of fourteen point two million dollars. Contingency covers known risks with responses: a permit delay, the battery lead time, and neighbor concerns. Management reserve covers unforeseen in-scope work, and senior management releases it. If contingency burns faster than progress, that is a governance signal: reassess it and tell Elena Vasquez. And if a spending threshold is missing for a decision above your authority, work with the sponsor to define it. Do not infer one.

3.title: Earned Value Measures
3.text: Earned value measures. Planned value is the authorized budget for scheduled work: what should be done. Earned value is the budget for work actually completed: what was done. Actual cost is the realized cost of the work performed. Cost variance is earned value minus actual cost: negative means over budget. Schedule variance is earned value minus planned value: negative means behind. The cost performance index is earned value over actual cost, and below one means over budget. The schedule performance index is earned value over planned value, and below one means behind.

3.title: Earned Value Curves
3.text: Here are the three curves. Planned value is the dashed curve: what should have been done by each date. Earned value is the green curve: the budget value of the work actually done. Actual cost is the red curve: what it cost. At the data date, earned value is below planned value, so the project is behind schedule. Earned value is also below actual cost, so it is over budget. Read the indices together: a cost index below one with a schedule index above one means schedule recovered at a cost.

3.title: Estimate at Completion
3.text: The estimate at completion has four formulas, and the assumption chooses. If current cost performance will continue, EAC equals BAC divided by CPI. If the variance was a one-off and future work goes at the planned rate, EAC equals actual cost plus BAC minus earned value. If the original plan is no longer valid, EAC equals actual cost plus a bottom-up estimate to complete. If both cost and schedule performance affect the remaining work, divide the remaining budget by CPI times SPI. Then ETC equals EAC minus AC, and VAC equals BAC minus EAC.

3.title: A Worked Earned Value Example
3.text: Work an example. BAC is one hundred, planned value fifty, earned value forty, actual cost forty-eight. Cost variance: forty minus forty-eight, negative eight. Schedule variance: forty minus fifty, negative ten. CPI: forty over forty-eight, about 0.83. SPI: forty over fifty, 0.80. If performance continues, EAC is one hundred divided by 0.83, about one hundred twenty. ETC is one-twenty minus forty-eight, seventy-two. VAC is negative twenty. The to-complete performance index is sixty over fifty-two, about 1.15. If that is unrealistic, forecast with the EAC.

3.title: Responding to a Financial Variance
3.text: When a financial variance appears, follow six steps. Compare it with the thresholds in the financial plan. Find the cause, and consider schedule performance too. Forecast with the right EAC, and check the to-complete index. Evaluate options: corrective action, scope or quality trade-offs through change control, reserves per protocol, schedule changes or additional funds. Escalate through governance when thresholds or authority are exceeded, bringing options. Update baselines and plans only through approved change requests, and communicate the forecast.

3.title: Anticipating Future Finance Challenges
3.text: Anticipate finance challenges. Inflation and exchange rates: include an inflation allowance and follow the plan's currency procedure. Resource cost and availability: plan resources early, because constraints raise cost. Contract type: a fixed-price contract shifts overrun risk to the seller, while time and materials keeps it with the buyer. Funding limits and timing: reconcile funding limits. Regulation: controls such as SOX or GDPR add cost, and compliance threats are risks. Life cycle cost: weigh operating and maintenance costs, not only project cost. Revenue shortfalls: track the business case.

3.title: Finance in Predictive, Agile and Hybrid Work
3.text: Finance differs by approach. Predictive: a full budget and cost baseline up front, with reserves. An S-curve, and lump sum or milestone funding. Earned value against the performance baseline. And change control for baseline changes. Agile: budget allocated by quarter or increment, and revised quarterly. A flatter spend curve, and incremental funding tied to value. Spend tracked per iteration against delivered value. And earned value in story points. Hybrid: a baseline for the fixed envelope and incremental funding for the iterative parts.

3.title: Finance Traps: What PMI Expects
3.text: The traps for finance. Forecast total cost with the estimate at completion, not the budget at completion and not the schedule index. Choose the formula by the assumption. The cost baseline excludes management reserve and changes only through change control. Contingency covers identified risks, while management reserve covers unknown unknowns. Reserve burning fast is a governance signal, so reassess and inform the sponsor. Read the cost and schedule indices together. And estimate all resource types, not only labor.

3.title: Module Recap
3.text: Let us recap the whole module. Scope: requirements, the statement, the work breakdown structure or backlog, control, and verify then validate. Schedule: logic, the critical path, float, compression, velocity, and baseline control. Cost: estimates, budget, baseline, reserves and funding. Earned value: planned value, earned value, actual cost, variances, indices and four formulas for the estimate at completion. And remember the constraints are linked. Now it is time to test yourself. Five questions follow. For each one, pause the video, choose your answer, and then listen to the explanation.

3.title: Practice Question 1
3.text: Question one. During a review, the project manager finds that an installation task listed in the signed scope statement is missing from the work breakdown structure. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C. Work that is already in the agreed scope is not a change, so it is added to the work breakdown structure and the related plans and documents are updated. A change request, a contract addition or leaving it out all treat an in-scope omission as something it is not.

3.title: Practice Question 2
3.text: Question two. A subcontractor's panels passed every inspection and test, but the customer has not formally accepted them. What should the project manager do next? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A. Verification confirms correctness, but the customer must formally accept the deliverable against the acceptance criteria, so the next step is a formal acceptance review. Closing on test results, repeating tests, or marking it accepted skips the customer's acceptance.

3.title: Practice Question 3
3.text: Question three. Several resources are over-allocated on activities that have float, and the finish date must not change. Which technique should the project manager use? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B. Smoothing uses free and total float only, so the critical path and finish date stay unchanged while the peaks are reduced. Leveling can change the critical path and delay the end date, and crashing and fast tracking spend money or add risk without need.

3.title: Practice Question 4
3.text: Question four. A project has a BAC of 200, an EV of 80 and an AC of 100. The cost overrun is expected to continue at the current rate. What is the EAC? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D. CPI is EV divided by AC, which is 0.8, and with current cost performance continuing, EAC equals BAC divided by CPI: 200 divided by 0.8 is 250. 220 treats the variance as a one-off, and the other values do not follow from any EAC formula for these numbers.

3.title: Practice Question 5
3.text: Question five. Halfway through the project, the contingency reserve has been used much faster than the work has progressed, and more risks are likely. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C. A reserve burning faster than progress is a governance signal, so the project manager reassesses its adequacy against remaining risks and tells the sponsor. Quietly topping up, hiding the use, or cutting testing avoid the governance conversation.

3.title: Answers at a Glance
3.text: Here are all five answers together. Question one: C. Work already in agreed scope is added to the WBS without a change request. Question two: A. Verified is not accepted, so hold a formal acceptance review. Question three: B. Smoothing uses float, so the end date stays put. Question four: D. BAC divided by CPI of 0.8 gives 250. Question five: C. A fast-burning reserve is a governance signal for the sponsor. That completes Module 7. Next, Module 8 covers quality, resource and procurement management. See you there.
